title: The homily
hook: the priest or deacon opens the readings for this crowd on this day
tomorrow: The Creed and the prayers of the faithful

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gospel: good news, greeted by standing and three small crosses. Your line was mind, lips, heart.

Ask people who grew up going to Mass about this part, and the stories come fast. The one who went on for forty minutes. The one who told the same joke every Easter. And the one, maybe once, who said something that landed so exactly on someone's week that they wondered if somebody had told him. It comes right after the Gospel, when the book has been kissed, the church settles back into the pews, and the priest or deacon begins to talk. Its name is older, and more interesting, than a speech.
screen: `THE STORIES PEOPLE TELL.` → `THE ONE THAT LANDED.` → `RIGHT AFTER THE GOSPEL.`

segments.voice: Homily comes from the Greek homilia: a conversation, a talk among people gathered together. Not a lecture from above. The verb shows up in a story you heard earlier on this path. On the road to Emmaus, two disciples are walking home, talking together about everything that has happened, and in Luke's Greek, their talking shares the same root. Then a stranger joins them and opens the scriptures to them. Later they say, in the Douay-Rheims: "Was not our heart burning within us, whilst he spoke in the way, and opened to us the scriptures?" That's what a homily is meant to do: take the readings everyone just heard and open them, for these people, on this day. Jesus did something like it in his hometown synagogue in Nazareth. He stood, read a passage from Isaiah, sat down, and with every eye on him said: "This day is fulfilled this scripture in your ears." Not a history lesson. Today. So a homily isn't a sermon on just any topic. The Church asks that it grow out of the readings and the Mass itself. It's given by a priest or deacon, and it's required on Sundays and holy days. Pope Francis wrote pages on homilies, asking that they be short, warm, and more like a mother talking to her children than a lecture. Afterward, the Church suggests a short silence, so what was said can settle. The word has been read; now it's handed to you, for this week.
screen: `HOMILIA: A CONVERSATION.` · `THE ROAD TO EMMAUS.` · `THIS DAY IS FULFILLED.` · `THE READINGS, FOR THESE PEOPLE.` · then, large: `WAS NOT OUR HEART BURNING WITHIN US?`

segments.voice: Think of the best sentence anyone ever said to you about life, from a pulpit, a classroom, a kitchen table, a friend at 2am; if nothing comes, take the one from Nazareth: this day is fulfilled. Ask what it would mean for today, this ordinary Tuesday or whatever day it is. If you pray, you can ask for ears to hear.
Homily. From the Greek for conversation: the priest or deacon opening the day's readings for the people in front of him. Today's word.
Your line: the word, for today. Old readings, opened for these people, this week. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 110 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE CREED AND THE PRAYERS OF THE FAITHFUL.`

howItsDone: After the Gospel, the congregation sits and the priest or deacon preaches the homily, drawn from the day's readings; it is required at Sunday and holy day Masses, and a short silence often follows.

original.note: Greek: a conversation, a talk among a gathered group, the root of homily.

trapdoor: what you thought: the priest's speech.
what it means: a conversation that opens the day's readings for these people, on this day.
what a scholar hears: homilia, from homilos, a gathered crowd; Luke uses the verb for the Emmaus disciples talking on the road. canon law reserves the homily to priests and deacons.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook rewritten so it no longer repeats day 108's 'X ends, and everyone sits down' opener, and no longer tells the listener what happened in their week ('everyone has a story', 'landed on your week').
Douay-Rheims Luke 24:32 and Luke 4:21 given from memory; confirm.
Luke 24:14–15 uses homileō for the disciples' talking; confirm.
Evangelii Gaudium 139–140 compares the homily to a mother speaking to her child; paraphrased. Confirm.
GIRM 66: homily by priest or deacon, required on Sundays and holy days of obligation; silence after (GIRM 66). Canon 767 §1 reserves it to priests and deacons. Confirm.
